title: Algebraic Fractions

findings.finding: Seven complete tasks recur unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copies repeat the same expressions or denominator pairs and require the same decisions, with no changed values, givens or required approach.
findings.checked: Compared complete student-visible tasks and their governing instructions. The matching pairs are p4-guided-d/p5-q1-e; p6-q2-a/p6-q2-e; p6-q2-b/p6-q2-f; p13-guided-r1-a/p14-q2-a; p13-guided-r1-b/p14-q2-c; p18-guided-g-node/p20-q3-b; and p18-guided-h-node/p20-q3-c. Excluded the other two pairs in c11: p19-q2 explicitly requires simplification before multiplication, whereas p18 guided practice only requests simplification. That changes the required approach, just as it does for the excluded p14-q4-a repetition. None of the retained copies belongs to an explicitly stated retrieval or comparison task.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice and exercises are completed in booklet order. Calculator use does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Remove p5-q1-e, p6-q2-e, p6-q2-f, p14-q2-a, p14-q2-c, p20-q3-b and p20-q3-c. Retain p19-q2-b and p19-q2-d because their instruction requires a different approach.

findings.doneWhen: Each retained duplicate pair has only its earlier copy, while questions explicitly requiring simplification before multiplication remain.

findings.finding: The multiplying topic's opening review omits products of two algebraic terms, which both introductory examples use directly.
findings.breakdown: The left example requires 2a × 3b = 6ab; the right requires 4x × 3x = 12x². The review checks only numerical multiplication of an algebraic term, so it does not reveal confusion between collecting like terms and multiplying them, particularly x × x versus 2x.
findings.checked: Searched all earlier teaching and the supplied preceding exercise. Earlier topics practise addition, subtraction and numerical rescaling of algebraic terms, not products of two algebraic terms. p12-q1 checks multiplication by numbers; p12-q4 checks cancellation, not forming products. The proposed items directly rehearse the two numerator products used in the examples and are short enough to append to the existing review.
findings.assumptions: Multiplication of algebraic terms is prior knowledge from introductory algebra and index work taught separately in the course. No calculator assumption is needed.

repair.proposal: Append to p12-q1-root: Simplify (g) 2a × 3b; (h) x × x; (i) 4x × 3x. Expected answers: 6ab, x², 12x².

findings.doneWhen: The opening review checks multiplication of distinct and repeated pronumerals before the introductory examples.

findings.finding: Generalise when a fixed algebraic sum simplifies to a positive whole-number multiple of x.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the existing reduction practice by asking students to explain which denominators divide the combined coefficient.
findings.checked: For positive integer n, the expression is 6x/n. Its coefficient is a positive integer exactly when n divides 6, giving n = 1, 2, 3, 6. This is an identity in x, so x = 0 does not introduce additional denominators. Addition, reduction and numerical divisibility suffice.
findings.assumptions: Students know factors of positive integers; no equation-solving method or calculator is required.

repair.proposal: After p5-q3-i, offer: For which positive integers n does 2x/n + 4x/n simplify to kx, with the same positive whole-number coefficient k for every x? Explain why your list is complete. Expected answer: 6x/n, so n must divide 6. Thus n = 1, 2, 3 or 6, giving 6x, 3x, 2x or x respectively.

findings.doneWhen: An optional task asks students to identify and justify all four denominators.

findings.finding: Generalise how independent changes to a rectangle's dimensions affect its area.
findings.breakdown: The task connects the unequal dimension changes in the netball and field questions with the repeated common multiplier in the square questions.
findings.checked: With positive dimensions l and w and positive factors r and s, the new area is (rl)(sw) = rslw. Since lw > 0, unchanged area requires rs = 1. For r = 2, s = 1/2. These calculations use algebraic multiplication and fraction operations already available by the topic's end.
findings.assumptions: All dimensions and scale factors are positive.

repair.proposal: After p16-q8-g, offer: A rectangle has positive length l and width w. Multiply its length by a positive factor r and its width by a positive factor s. Express its new area. What condition on r and s keeps its area unchanged? If its length doubles, what must happen to its width? Expected answers: rslw; rs = 1; the width must be halved.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task elicits the area multiplier rs and explains the reciprocal relationship needed to preserve area.

findings.finding: Contrast multiplication and division using a fixed first operand and a reciprocal pair.
findings.breakdown: An explicit prediction and comparison can expose the equivalence between dividing by a fraction and multiplying by its reciprocal. The existing mixed-operation questions apply the rule but do not provide this comparison run.
findings.checked: The four results are 2x/15, 5x/6, 2x/15 and 5x/6 in the revised order. Consecutive items change only the operation or only the second operand. Equality is requested as an identity for every x, avoiding the exceptional coincidence of all four values at x = 0. The follow-up gives (3a/7)(14/9) = 2a/3. All denominators and divisors are nonzero numerical constants.
findings.assumptions: x and a may be any real numbers. Only the taught multiplication and reciprocal methods are needed.

repair.proposal: After p20-q4 and before the contextual questions, ask students to predict which expressions are equal for every x before simplifying: (1) x/3 × 2/5; (2) x/3 ÷ 2/5; (3) x/3 ÷ 5/2; (4) x/3 × 5/2. Expected answers: 2x/15, 5x/6, 2x/15, 5x/6. Ask students to explain the matching pairs. Keep the first operand fixed; change one feature between consecutive items. Follow with 3a/7 ÷ 9/14, giving 2a/3.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict, calculate and explain the matching pairs, then apply the relationship to an unpatterned question.

findings.finding: Investigate when reversing a division preserves its value.
findings.breakdown: Students use reciprocals to explain the effect of operand order rather than perform another routine division.
findings.checked: For positive fractions A and B, the quotients are A/B and B/A and their product is 1. If the quotients are equal, their common positive value must be 1, so A = B; conversely A = B makes both quotients 1. Positivity excludes zero divisors and the additional negative case. Fraction multiplication, division and squaring are available by the topic's end.
findings.assumptions: A and B are positive fractions.

repair.proposal: After p21-q7, offer: Let A and B be positive fractions. Write expressions for A ÷ B and B ÷ A. What is their product? When are their values equal? Explain using fraction operations. Expected answer: A/B and B/A; their product is 1; they are equal exactly when A = B, when both values are 1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks for both the reciprocal-product relationship and a justified equality condition.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the common denominator leaves the numerator-combination step unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: The common denominator changes from 1 to 4.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numerators x and 2x and the addition operation.

protectedGroups.observation: Adding and subtracting the same fractional multiple place the result on opposite sides of pi.
protectedGroups.invariant: The whole term pi and fractional term pi/4.

protectedGroups.observation: Repeats the addition/subtraction contrast with another denominator.
protectedGroups.invariant: The whole term pi and fractional term pi/6.

protectedGroups.observation: Subtracting a smaller fraction of pi leaves a larger result.
protectedGroups.varies: The denominator of the subtracted unit fraction.
protectedGroups.invariant: The starting amount 2pi, subtraction and numerator pi.

protectedGroups.observation: Adding one half, two thirds and three quarters of pi produces progressively larger totals.
protectedGroups.invariant: The starting amount pi and addition.

protectedGroups.observation: Multiplying each side by a factor multiplies the area by its square; a side factor greater than one-half can still produce an area less than one-half.
protectedGroups.invariant: The original square has side x and area x².

protectedGroups.observation: Repeated side reductions compound, and the area exponent is twice the number of reductions.
protectedGroups.varies: The number of successive reductions: one, two and n.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each reduction multiplies both side lengths by 3/5.

importReview: Lean content review table: 60 of 60 blocks passed.

dropped.reason: The suggestion's requirement that the practice lack such a run is defeated by p4-guided-a through p4-guided-c. They retain the numerator structure x + 2x while varying the common denominator through 1, 4 and 3, exposing a whole term, an unreduced fraction and reduction to a whole term. p4-guided-e/f and p5-q3 further practise reduction.

candidates.finding: Hold the numerators fixed while varying the common denominator to expose when further reduction is possible.

dropped.reason: The unchanged-whole-task test fails: p10-q5 explicitly requires a single fraction and supplies the whole-term conversion reminder 4x = 4x/1, whereas p7-guided-c supplies neither. The expression repeats, but its student-visible support and governing instruction are changed.

candidates.finding: p10-q5-r1c2 repeats the complete simplification task 3x + x/2 from p7-guided-c without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct: for an identity in x, 3a + 2b = 18 gives the positive integer pairs (2,6) and (4,3). Dropped under the four-suggestion limit; the retained suggestions more directly expose fraction reduction, area multiplication and reciprocal relationships without shifting attention to an integer-solution search.

candidates.finding: Generalise when two algebraic fractions with fixed denominators combine to a whole multiple of x.

dropped.reason: The sharp-jump test fails. p16-q8-a through p16-q8-d repeatedly establish the squared relationship between side and area, including halving sides and comparing a scaled area with one-half. Part e reverses that established relationship as a challenge within the closing exercise. The irrational answer follows from the assumed prior square-root knowledge; it does not establish several simultaneous unsupported changes. No bridge is required at the high-severity threshold.

candidates.finding: p16-q8-e jumps from calculating and comparing areas for given side multipliers to finding an unknown irrational divisor.
